opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, honestly. The way I tend to frame it: a metric is only useful insofar as it's a faithful proxy for the thing you actually care about. And the trouble is that in machine learning we very often don't know precisely what we care about, or we care about something that's really hard to measure directly, so we grab something convenient and then slowly forget that it was ever a proxy.

So the first test I apply is pretty simple: if I improve this number, does the thing I care about actually get better? And does that hold up when people start optimizing for it? Goodhart's law is real. A benchmark that tracked capability nicely when nobody was tuning against it can become almost meaningless once the whole field has been hill-climbing on it for a few years. You see papers squeezing out a tenth of a point, and you have to ask whether that tenth of a point corresponds to anything in the world.

The second thing I look at is whether the metric is honest about cost. In efficiency work especially, people love to report things like parameter count or theoretical FLOPs because they're clean and easy to compute. But if what you care about is "can I train this faster" or "can I serve this cheaper," then what matters is wall-clock time and dollars on real hardware. A sparse model with ninety percent fewer parameters that runs no faster on a GPU hasn't saved anybody anything. So I try to ask: who is the person who would actually use this result, and what would they measure?

Third, I care about variance and reproducibility. A metric that swings by more than your claimed improvement across random seeds isn't telling you much. I've been bitten by that myself. You run something once, it looks great, you run it five more times and the effect is gone. So part of judging a metric is understanding its noise floor before you trust any comparison made with it.

And finally, I think it's healthy to be a little suspicious of any single number. Usually the right move is a small set of metrics that check each other: accuracy plus cost, in-distribution plus out-of-distribution, an automated score plus some actual human judgment of outputs. If they all point the same way, great. If they disagree, that disagreement is often the most interesting thing you'll learn.

So, short version: a good metric is one that still tracks what you care about after people try hard to game it, that reflects real costs, and whose noise you understand. Most metrics fail at least one of those, and that's fine, as long as we remember it.

r001.rationale: The response offers several tests for useful metrics but does not state that there is no clear general rule.

r002.rationale: It discusses proxy fidelity, costs, and noise, but does not identify non-vacuity as a criterion for choosing measurements.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first question I ask is: what decision would I make differently depending on the value of this metric? If the answer is "none," then it's not really a metric, it's just a number. A useful metric has to be connected to something you actually care about, and you should be able to articulate what that thing is before you start measuring.

The second thing I look for is whether the metric survives contact with people trying to optimize it. This is the classic Goodhart problem, and it's rampant in machine learning. Accuracy on a benchmark is a wonderful proxy for "does this model understand the task" right up until the moment the entire field starts tuning against it, and then it becomes a proxy for "how good is this lab at hill-climbing on this particular dataset." So I try to ask: if I handed this metric to a very motivated grad student and said "make this number go up," would the thing they build actually be better in the way I care about? Or would they find a shortcut that satisfies the metric and nothing else?

The third piece, and I think this one gets undervalued, is whether the metric is cheap and reliable enough that people will actually use it correctly. A lot of my work on the lottery ticket hypothesis was about sparsity, and there were these enormous debates about what counts as a good sparse network. You can measure parameter count, you can measure FLOPs, you can measure wall-clock time on specific hardware. The honest answer is wall-clock time on the hardware you're going to deploy on, but that's expensive and noisy and depends on things outside the model. So people reach for parameter count because it's easy, and then you get papers claiming big wins that don't translate into anything real. The question isn't just "is this metric correct," it's "is this metric correct in the way it will actually be used in practice, by people with deadlines."

And then, honestly, I've become a lot more skeptical of single numbers over the years. When I was at MosaicML and now at Databricks, the thing that actually mattered to customers was never one eval score. It was "does this model do my task, on my data, at a cost I can afford." The best metrics I've seen tend to be ones that are close to the real use case and that you look at alongside several others, rather than one leaderboard number you stare at in isolation. If someone shows me a result that only moves one metric and I can't tell a story for why that should matter downstream, I get nervous. If I see something move three or four metrics that measure genuinely different things, that's when I start to believe it.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what do you actually care about? A metric is a proxy for something, and it’s easy to forget that and start treating the number as the thing itself. If I care about whether a model is useful to someone, accuracy on a benchmark might tell me something about that, but it’s not the whole story.

So I’d ask: when this metric improves, does the thing I care about actually get better? And can I come up with a way to improve the metric without improving that underlying thing? That second question is a really useful sanity check. If you can get a better score by doing something that’s clearly unhelpful, you’ve found a limitation of the metric.

That doesn’t necessarily mean you throw it away. It means you understand what evidence it gives you and where you need to look beyond it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what decision are you trying to make with it? A metric is useful if it helps you make that decision better. It’s not enough that it’s easy to compute or that everyone reports it.

Take accuracy. That can be a perfectly reasonable metric, but if the mistakes your model makes have very different costs, then averaging them all together may hide exactly what you care about. Similarly, if you’re trying to make a model faster, counting operations might be a useful proxy, but ultimately you should check whether it actually runs faster in the setting where you’ll use it.

So I tend to ask: what is this metric a proxy for, what does it leave out, and can you improve the number without improving the thing you actually wanted? That last question is especially revealing. Once you start optimizing a metric, you find out pretty quickly where the gap is between the measurement and the goal.
